For 2025 to 2026 Lynchburg taxes real estate at $0.84 per $100 of total assessed value. Because City Council sets it, check the figure for the year you sell. The City Assessor page carries the details, and a ParcelViewer map tool there shows property records.

The office is open Monday through Friday, 8:30 am to 5 pm.

Worth is the Assessor's call. Mailing the bill and accepting your check is the Treasurer's. The Assessor operates under Chapter 18-48 of the Lynchburg City Code, Title 58.1 of the Code of Virginia and Article X of the state Constitution, and keeps an alphabetical ownership tax roll for each July 1 to June 30 period.

Every parcel is reassessed every two years, so a Lynchburg owner can see a value change without making any improvement. Transfers and building permits are handled all year, so a new deck or a sale can shift a record between reassessments. The office also prepares special appraisal estimates for budgeting and rental studies from time to time, and those are separate from your tax bill.

Get the next installment date from the Treasurer and the appeal window from the Assessor.

Start with the Assessor, whose office page has an Appeals section. State law adds a correction route in Va. Code 58.1-3980, aimed at mistakes by the assessing official or factual errors that came out of a general reassessment.

  • The correction request goes to the official who made the assessment.
  • You get three years past the end of the tax year, or one year past the assessment date if that is later, to ask.
  • For real estate the statute applies only when the error is the assessor's or a factual error made during reassessment.
  • A disagreement about value alone follows the city's own review process, which the Assessor can explain.

Keep photos, repair bids and comparable sales ready, since any appeal rests on evidence.

Virginia puts a real estate tax lien first among all liens. That is the reason a closing agent takes delinquent tax straight from the seller's proceeds. Under Va. Code 58.1-3340, whoever buys at a sale, or a foreclosure trustee, must put proceeds toward assessed taxes and levies, penalties and interest among them.

The treasurer lifts the lien once the money arrives. Splitting the current year with the buyer is a matter for your contract. Va. Code 58.1-802 also levies the grantor's tax: 50 cents on each $500 of consideration. The seller owes it unless the parties agree otherwise, and the court clerk takes payment at recording.

Thinking about a quick sale? Ask the Treasurer for the precise payoff, and let the title company double-check for liens before you put pen to paper.

sections.h2: Why your value can change between cycles
sections.html:
Cycles are not the whole story. A sale that goes through, or a building permit that is finished, can prompt the office to update the record at any time. If you built a deck last spring and the record changed afterward, that is the process working as designed rather than a mistake. A change you did not cause is different. Check the ParcelViewer record for square footage, bedroom and bath counts and lot size, and hold it up against the house you really own. A data mistake is the simplest kind to fix.

Winter and summer both matter to inspectors. Winters average 35.9 degrees F in January and Julys 76.0 degrees F. A typical year brings roughly 27.4 days of 90 degrees or higher and 11.6 inches of snow. Note the age and state of the roof and furnace before the first showing.

Remember that exempt parcels, about 1,645 of them, are carved out of the roll. Exemption or program status on your parcel? Ask the Assessor whether it survives a sale.

sections.h2: A short checklist before you list
sections.html:
1. Look up your parcel on ParcelViewer and confirm the details are right.
  2. Phone the Treasurer at the city for the next installment date and any balance.
  3. If the value looks high, ring the Assessor on 434-455-3830 and ask about the appeal window.
  4. Collect photos, repair bids and comparable sales in one folder.
  5. Ask the title company to start a lien search early, so nothing surprises you near closing.

That order puts the cheap questions first. A phone call to the Treasurer costs nothing and tells you more about your closing costs than any estimate.

The city's tax period runs July 1 to June 30, which means a house sold mid-year has a tax year that is only partly used. Your contract decides how the months are divided, and the settlement agent turns that into a line on your statement. Ask to see the dates used. Say the first installment is already paid: the buyer then usually repays you for the rest of that year. If an installment is still open, the agent will usually deduct your share from your proceeds and pay the Treasurer.

Expect the deed charge as its own line on the statement, borne by the seller unless your contract says otherwise. Because the clerk collects it at recording, you will see it as a charge at the table rather than on a city bill.

sections.h2: What buyers ask about Lynchburg houses
sections.html:
Expect questions about the slope of the lot. On a hilly street a long driveway, a steep yard or an old retaining wall can matter more to a buyer than the kitchen. Repair loose stone or a leaning wall if you can, and be ready to say who built it.

Kemper Street Station handles both Amtrak and Greyhound, and Lynchburg Regional Airport has American Eagle service to Charlotte, which helps buyers who travel. Say so in your listing notes if your street is close to either.

Students and staff from Liberty University, the University of Lynchburg and Randolph College make up part of the rental and buyer pool near campuses, and hospitals such as Lynchburg General and Virginia Baptist draw medical workers. Commuters use U.S. 29, U.S. 501, U.S. 221 and U.S. 460, and the Lynchburg Expressway moves traffic across town. Amtrak and Greyhound stop at Kemper Street Station.

A cash sale needs no lender, so it moves quickly. You request an offer, the buyer views the house in its current condition, and a title company prepares the deed, clears the tax and files the paperwork with the circuit court clerk. Start by collecting the latest tax bill, any Assessor notice and the names on the deed. Where the owner has died, say so early, since a personal representative's authority must be documented before anyone can sign a deed.

Set on the James River in the Blue Ridge foothills, Lynchburg is an independent city. The population was 79,009 in 2020 and is estimated at 81,347 for 2025. Its nickname, the City of Seven Hills, describes terrain that shapes lot lines, driveways and retaining walls. Floods struck in 1842, 1847, 1870 and 1877, so a house close to the river needs a harder look at drainage than one up on a ridge.

The city has ten recognized historic districts, four of them in the downtown residential area. Court House Hill-Downtown, Daniel's Hill, Diamond Hill, Federal Hill, Garland Hill and Rivermont are on the list. Before selling or renovating inside a district, ask city planning staff which review applies. Buyers rely on U.S. routes, because no Interstate reaches Lynchburg, the state's largest city without one.

faqs.q: What is the Lynchburg property tax rate?
faqs.a: The City Assessor's page lists $0.84 per $100 of assessed value for 2025 to 2026. City Council sets the rate, so confirm it for the current year.

faqs.q: How often does Lynchburg reassess property?
faqs.a: All parcels are reassessed every two years. Transfers and building permits are processed throughout the year.

faqs.q: Where is the Lynchburg City Assessor's office?
faqs.a: It is at 900 Church Street, Lynchburg, VA 24504, phone 434-455-3830, open Monday through Friday from 8:30 am to 5 pm.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Lynchburg house with property tax owed?
faqs.a: Yes. The tax lien is paid from the sale proceeds at closing, and the treasurer releases it. Get a payoff figure first so the title company can plan for it.

faqs.q: Where do I find Lynchburg due dates and appeal deadlines?
faqs.a: Call the City Treasurer for due dates and the City Assessor for appeal deadlines.
